name: Fascia lata

bony_attachments.landmark: via iliotibial tract to Gerdy's tubercle

compartment_contents: all thigh muscles (subdivided by its 3 intermuscular septa)
function: Dense tubular deep fascia of the thigh; its lateral thickening (iliotibial tract) is the strongest fascial structure in the body, tensioned by gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae to stabilize the knee in stance.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Iliotibial (IT) tract/band
function: Lateral thickening of fascia lata; acts as a tension member stabilizing the hip and knee during single-leg stance/gait, and (per Stecco) as a myofascial force-transmission pathway linking gluteus maximus and TFL to the tibia.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Anterior (lateral) intermuscular septum of the thigh
function: Separates the anterior (quadriceps, femoral n.) from the posterior (hamstring, sciatic n.) thigh compartment laterally.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Medial intermuscular septum of the thigh
function: Separates the anterior compartment from the medial (adductor, obturator n.) compartment.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Posterior intermuscular septum of the thigh
function: Separates the medial (adductor) from the posterior (hamstring) compartment.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Anterior osteofascial compartment of the thigh
function: Contains the hip flexors/knee extensors, all femoral-nerve innervated.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Medial (adductor) osteofascial compartment of the thigh
function: Contains the hip adductors, predominantly obturator-nerve innervated (adductor magnus's hamstring part is the documented exception, sciatic-innervated).
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Posterior (hamstring) osteofascial compartment of the thigh
function: Contains the hamstrings, sciatic-nerve innervated.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Crural (deep) fascia of the leg
function: Dense tubular deep fascia of the leg, thickened proximally (forms part of the pes anserinus attachment) and distally into the ankle retinacula; gives origin to superficial fibers of several leg muscles directly from its deep surface.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Anterior intermuscular septum of the leg
function: Separates the anterior compartment from the lateral (fibular) compartment.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Posterior intermuscular septum of the leg (transverse crural septum)
function: Separates the superficial from the deep posterior compartment.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Interosseous membrane (leg)
function: Fibrous sheet linking tibia and fibula; separates the anterior from the deep posterior compartment, transmits load from fibula to tibia, gives origin to deep muscle fibers (tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior, EHL, FHL).
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Anterior osteofascial compartment of the leg
function: Ankle/toe dorsiflexors, deep-fibular-nerve innervated. Tightly enclosed by unyielding fascia -- classic site of acute compartment syndrome after tibial fracture.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Lateral osteofascial compartment of the leg
function: Ankle evertors, superficial-fibular-nerve innervated.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Superficial posterior osteofascial compartment of the leg
function: Primary ankle plantarflexors.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Deep posterior osteofascial compartment of the leg
function: Toe flexors + tibialis posterior, tibial-nerve innervated.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Flexor retinaculum (of the ankle, forms the tarsal tunnel)
function: Roofs the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus; compression here (tarsal tunnel syndrome) affects the tibial nerve, analogous to carpal tunnel syndrome in the wrist.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Extensor retinaculum (superior + inferior, of the ankle)
function: Prevents bowstringing of the anterior compartment tendons during ankle dorsiflexion; analogous in function to the wrist's extensor retinaculum.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: (Superior + inferior) fibular (peroneal) retinaculum
function: Retains the fibularis tendons behind the lateral malleolus.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Plantar aponeurosis (fascia)
function: Thick central band of the plantar fascia supporting the medial longitudinal arch; the 'windlass mechanism' -- toe dorsiflexion tensions the aponeurosis and passively raises the arch during late stance/push-off. A classically overuse-injured structure (plantar fasciitis).
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Fibrous flexor sheaths (toes, annular + cruciate pulleys)

bony_attachments.landmark: plantar surface of each phalanx and MTP/IP joint plates

function: Osteofibrous tunnels analogous to the hand's, keeping the long toe flexor tendons apposed to bone through the gait cycle.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell) ch.6; Stecco C, Functional Atlas of the Human Fascial System (2015), Churchill Livingstone -- lower limb fascial continuity chapters; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Lateral intermuscular septum of the thigh

bony_attachments.landmark: lateral lip of the linea aspera

function: Runs from the fascia lata to the linea aspera, separating vastus lateralis in front from the short head of biceps femoris behind. The strongest of the thigh septa, and the deep anchor of the iliotibial tract.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Adductor (Hunter's/subsartorial) canal

bony_attachments.landmark: runs along the medial thigh from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus

function: An aponeurotic tunnel roofed by the vasto-adductor membrane, bounded by vastus medialis, adductor longus and magnus, and sartorius. The target of the adductor canal block, which reaches the saphenous nerve while largely sparing the quadriceps, so patients can still weight-bear after knee arthroplasty. Block placed too proximally catches the nerve to vastus medialis and loses that advantage.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Femoral sheath

bony_attachments.landmark: continuous above with transversalis and iliac fascia at the inguinal ligament

function: A funnel of transversalis and iliac fascia drawn into the thigh behind the inguinal ligament, divided into three compartments. The femoral NERVE lies outside it, which is why a femoral sheath injection does not block the nerve.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Femoral canal

bony_attachments.landmark: lacunar ligament medially, pectineal ligament posteriorly

function: The medial compartment of the femoral sheath, whose upper opening is the femoral ring. Its narrow, sharp-edged boundaries are why a femoral hernia strangulates far more readily than an inguinal one. It lies BELOW and LATERAL to the pubic tubercle, the sign that distinguishes it from an inguinal hernia.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Popliteal fascia

bony_attachments.landmark: continuous above with the fascia lata
continuous below with the crural fascia

function: A tough roof over the popliteal fossa, pierced by the small saphenous vein. Its rigidity is what makes a Baker's cyst expand distally into the calf rather than superficially, and what allows a ruptured cyst to mimic deep vein thrombosis.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Tendinous arch of soleus

bony_attachments.landmark: posterior surface of the head and neck

function: The fibrous arch between the tibial and fibular origins of soleus. The tibial nerve and popliteal vessels pass beneath it into the deep posterior compartment; it is a recognised site of popliteal artery entrapment and of tibial nerve compression.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Iliopsoas bursa and its fascial covering

bony_attachments.landmark: iliopubic eminence, between the tendon and the hip capsule

function: The largest bursa in the body, lying between the iliopsoas tendon and the hip capsule and communicating with the joint in a substantial minority of people. That communication is why a hip effusion can present as a groin mass, and the plane in which the tendon snaps in internal snapping hip.
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

name: Medial (hallucal) compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the great toe's intrinsic abductor and flexor along the medial plantar border.
notes: Bounded by the medial intermuscular septum of the sole; the plantar-most site checked for tenderness/tightness in suspected foot compartment syndrome after a calcaneal fracture or crush injury.

name: Lateral compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the little toe's intrinsic abductor and flexor along the lateral plantar border.
notes: Mirrors the medial compartment on the fibular side of the sole, bounded by the lateral intermuscular septum.

name: Central (calcaneal) compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the superficial and deep central plantar muscles, the tendons of flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus, and the lateral plantar neurovascular bundle.
notes: The largest and least distensible of the foot compartments -- some schemes split it into superficial and deep (calcaneal) sub-compartments -- and clinically the one most often requiring fasciotomy after a calcaneal fracture, since the calcaneal branch of the lateral plantar artery runs through it.

name: Interosseous compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the dorsal and plantar interossei between the metatarsals.
notes: Four separate intermetatarsal spaces surgically, grouped here as one entry; accessed dorsally rather than plantarly during fasciotomy, unlike the other three foot compartments.

name: Medial (hallucal) compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the great toe's intrinsic abductor and flexor along the medial plantar border.
notes: Bounded by the medial intermuscular septum of the sole; the plantar-most site checked for tenderness/tightness in suspected foot compartment syndrome after a calcaneal fracture or crush injury.

name: Lateral compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the little toe's intrinsic abductor and flexor along the lateral plantar border.
notes: Mirrors the medial compartment on the fibular side of the sole, bounded by the lateral intermuscular septum.

name: Central (calcaneal) compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the superficial and deep central plantar muscles, the tendons of flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus, and the lateral plantar neurovascular bundle.
notes: The largest and least distensible of the foot compartments -- some schemes split it into superficial and deep (calcaneal) sub-compartments -- and clinically the one most often requiring fasciotomy after a calcaneal fracture, since the calcaneal branch of the lateral plantar artery runs through it.

name: Interosseous compartment of the foot
source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Manoli A, Weber TG, Foot Ankle 10:340 (1990) [foot compartment model]
function: Encloses the dorsal and plantar interossei between the metatarsals.
